title: Horace Silver audition and race in the business
summary: His audition for Horace Silver ends with the warning that a white drummer would cost the band work, followed by parallels with Goodman and Artie Shaw.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Did you ever witness any racial incidents or that kind of thing in your career? I know as you said, your time in the business was supposedly a little after much of that was worked out.
Yeah I had one. I auditioned with Horace Silver. He just died by the way. Randy Brecker was on the band, Bennie Maupin, I can’t remember the bass player, and Horace. And so

they were holding auditions up at Lynn Oliver’s studio. Mike Garson got me the audition. He was David Bowie’s conductor for, I don’t know, forever. And I went up there and I played first. And I was the only white guy auditioning on drums. Billy Cobham was leaving and a replacement was being held for him. I mean auditions were taking place. And one guy played, a black guy played. And he wasn’t particularly good. He wasn’t very good. But Horace was nice about it, and let him play a couple of tunes. Then called me up, and I played about four or five tunes with him. And then everybody’s sitting over there. Then another black guy comes up to play drums. Better than the first, but not particularly good. Then he said, “Danny, why don’t you come on up and play some more.” So I played another three or four tunes with Horace Silver. So now Mike Garson is there and we’re waiting to go down to Dave Liebman’s loft to have a session, but we’re waiting for Randy Brecker to come down. Now Bennie Maupin, the tenor player, who had been with Head Hunters during my first sitting down to play the drums, had walked to the other end of the studio and played against the wall. Wouldn’t come up on the stand and play with me. But when Horace called me up the second time, he came up on the — it was a little raised platform at Lynn Oliver’s studio, and did play with me. And Randy Brecker, now we’re waiting for Randy downstairs, it’s like a half an hour man. You know and we’re going down to Liebman’s. And he said, “Horace wants to hire you, man,” but he says, “he knows if he puts a white drummer on this band,” he said, “it’s going to cost him about 40 percent of his work.”

Because they had a band meeting up there. He said, “he wants to use you but he can’t.” So we went down and the next morning I’m staying at Mike Garson’s and the phone rings and Mike says, “Danny, it’s Horace Silver.” And I said, “what?” I mean I must have got the gig, Horace Silver’s calling me. And you don’t forget it when you get a call from Horace Silver. He said, “Danny, it was obvious you were far superior to all those other drummers there. But there’s one other guy I want to hear in Philadelphia.” And that guy lasted about a week. But I felt a draft as you would say. Now I’m not saying that I would have lasted a week either, but at least I play better than the guys that were there.
It’s ironic because they told Benny Goodman the same thing — you’re going to lose 40 percent of your work if you hire Lionel Hampton or whatever.

Artie Shaw had that whole scene when he had Hot Lips Page and he couldn’t even do a southern tour unless Hot Lips was at least like ten feet away from the rest of the band. He turned down a whole southern tour. And Billie Holiday was with that band too and there
were some problems along those lines too. But I mean other than that I can’t say there’s been an awful lot as far as I’m concerned with the black and white thing.
